Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80
  - Security config matches stable (no explicit securityContext)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine
  - Selector: app=recommendation-engine (removed version constraint) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1
  - Preserved port mapping: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Result (approx 50/50 traffic)
- Pods behind the Service:
  - engine-v2-0: 2 pods (stable)
  - engine-v2-1: 2 pods (canary)
- Endpoints now list 4 pod IPs on port 8080 (2 stable + 2 canary), yielding ~50% traffic to the canary.

Notes
- To adjust weighting, change replica counts (e.g., canary 1/stable 3 ≈ 25% canary).
- To roll back quickly, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0 (or delete/scale down engine-v2-1).

service/recommendation-engine created

Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80
  - Security config matches stable (no explicit securityContext)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine
  - Selector: app=recommendation-engine (removed version constraint) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1
  - Preserved port mapping: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Result (approx 50/50 traffic)
- Pods behind the Service:
  - engine-v2-0: 2 pods (stable)
  - engine-v2-1: 2 pods (canary)
- Endpoints now list 4 pod IPs on port 8080 (2 stable + 2 canary), yielding ~50% traffic to the canary.

Notes
- To adjust weighting, change replica counts (e.g., canary 1/stable 3 ≈ 25% canary).
- To roll back quickly, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0 (or delete/scale down engine-v2-1).

What I changed
- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80

Result (approx 50/50 traffic)
- Pods behind the Service:
  - engine-v2-0: 2 pods (stable)
  - engine-v2-1: 2 pods (canary)
- Endpoints now list 4 pod IPs on port 8080 (2 stable + 2 canary), yielding ~50% traffic to the canary.

Notes
- To adjust weighting, change replica counts (e.g., canary 1/stable 3 ≈ 25% canary).
- To roll back quickly, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0 (or delete/scale down engine-v2-1).

  - args: ["-g", "daemon off;"]

- Deployment crashloop-test/app reports Available=True, ReadyReplicas=1, NewReplicaSetAvailable.

- Add liveness/readiness probes for nginx.
- Expose it via a Service/Ingress.
- Roll back to the previous revision (kubectl rollout undo) if needed.

Steps.message:
I fixed it.

What was wrong:
- The container in the Deployment was started with command: /bin/sh -c and args: nonexistent_command, which caused the pod to crash-loop.

What I changed:
- Updated the Deployment crashloop-test/app to run nginx properly:
  - command: ["nginx"]
  - args: ["-g", "daemon off;"]
  - kept replicas and labels the same; set imagePullPolicy to IfNotPresent.

Verification:
- Pod crashloop-test/app-86cbb87c6b-p8mhx is 1/1 Running.
- Deployment crashloop-test/app reports Available=True, ReadyReplicas=1, NewReplicaSetAvailable.

If you want, I can:
- Add liveness/readiness probes for nginx.
- Expose it via a Service/Ingress.
- Roll back to the previous revision (kubectl rollout undo) if needed.

I fixed it.

What was wrong:
- The container in the Deployment was started with command: /bin/sh -c and args: nonexistent_command, which caused the pod to crash-loop.

- Updated the Deployment crashloop-test/app to run nginx properly:
  - command: ["nginx"]
  - args: ["-g", "daemon off;"]
  - kept replicas and labels the same; set imagePullPolicy to IfNotPresent.

Verification:
- Pod crashloop-test/app-86cbb87c6b-p8mhx is 1/1 Running.
- Deployment crashloop-test/app reports Available=True, ReadyReplicas=1, NewReplicaSetAvailable.

If you want, I can:
- Add liveness/readiness probes for nginx.
- Expose it via a Service/Ingress.
- Roll back to the previous revision (kubectl rollout undo) if needed.

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

Root cause:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc". Scheduler event: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims. storageclass.storage.k8s.io 'sc' not found”.

What I changed:
- Deleted the pending PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since it wasn’t bound).
- Recreated homepage-pvc using the existing StorageClass "standard" (the cluster default).

Current state:
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, ReadWriteOnce).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster (container nginx is ready).

Notes for future:
- Use storageClassName: standard (or omit storageClassName to use the default) instead of a non-existent class.
- If you specifically need a class named "sc", we can create it, but updating storageClassName on an existing PVC is not allowed—you must recreate the PVC.

Want me to expose the pod with a Service or verify the mounted volume contents?

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I fixed it.

Root cause:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc". Scheduler event: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims. storageclass.storage.k8s.io 'sc' not found”.

What I changed:
- Deleted the pending PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since it wasn’t bound).
- Recreated homepage-pvc using the existing StorageClass "standard" (the cluster default).

Current state:
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, ReadWriteOnce).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster (container nginx is ready).

Notes for future:
- Use storageClassName: standard (or omit storageClassName to use the default) instead of a non-existent class.
- If you specifically need a class named "sc", we can create it, but updating storageClassName on an existing PVC is not allowed—you must recreate the PVC.

Want me to expose the pod with a Service or verify the mounted volume contents?

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

Root cause:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc". Scheduler event: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims. storageclass.storage.k8s.io 'sc' not found”.

What I changed:
- Deleted the pending PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since it wasn’t bound).
- Recreated homepage-pvc using the existing StorageClass "standard" (the cluster default).

Current state:
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, ReadWriteOnce).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster (container nginx is ready).

Notes for future:
- Use storageClassName: standard (or omit storageClassName to use the default) instead of a non-existent class.
- If you specifically need a class named "sc", we can create it, but updating storageClassName on an existing PVC is not allowed—you must recreate the PVC.

Want me to expose the pod with a Service or verify the mounted volume contents?

results.taskOutput:
I found the pod was Running but not Ready because the health probes were misconfigured.

What I did:
- Diagnosis:
  - Pod webapp was failing readiness/liveness: HTTP GET /is_ready and /get_status on port 80 returned connection refused.
  - quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80) and serves “/” by default; those custom paths don’t exist.
- Fix:
  - Updated the Deployment to use port 8080 (named http) and changed both probes to GET / on port http.
  - Updated the Service to targetPort http (8080).

Current status:
- Pod webapp-68d6b98486-r9fc2 is 1/1 Running and Ready.
- Service endpoints are healthy and pointing to port 8080.

If you need external access (outside the cluster), there’s no Ingress/Route configured yet. Tell me the hostname you want and I can create an Ingress (or switch the Service to NodePort/LoadBalancer) to expose it.

I found the pod was Running but not Ready because the health probes were misconfigured.

What I did:
- Diagnosis:
  - Pod webapp was failing readiness/liveness: HTTP GET /is_ready and /get_status on port 80 returned connection refused.
  - quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80) and serves “/” by default; those custom paths don’t exist.
- Fix:
  - Updated the Deployment to use port 8080 (named http) and changed both probes to GET / on port http.
  - Updated the Service to targetPort http (8080).

- Pod webapp-68d6b98486-r9fc2 is 1/1 Running and Ready.
- Service endpoints are healthy and pointing to port 8080.

outputSteps.content:
I found the pod was Running but not Ready because the health probes were misconfigured.

What I did:
- Diagnosis:
  - Pod webapp was failing readiness/liveness: HTTP GET /is_ready and /get_status on port 80 returned connection refused.
  - quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80) and serves “/” by default; those custom paths don’t exist.
- Fix:
  - Updated the Deployment to use port 8080 (named http) and changed both probes to GET / on port http.
  - Updated the Service to targetPort http (8080).

Current status:
- Pod webapp-68d6b98486-r9fc2 is 1/1 Running and Ready.
- Service endpoints are healthy and pointing to port 8080.

If you need external access (outside the cluster), there’s no Ingress/Route configured yet. Tell me the hostname you want and I can create an Ingress (or switch the Service to NodePort/LoadBalancer) to expose it.

  Current (before fix) rule: apiGroups: ["apps"], resources: ["deployments"], verbs: ["list"]

- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to allow reading Pods in the core API group:
  - apiGroups: [""]
  - resources: ["pods"]
  - verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already points to this Role and the pod-reader ServiceAccount, so no changes were needed there.

  kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods

  kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing Deployments in the apps API group. It did not grant any permissions on Pods (which are in the core API group "").
  Current (before fix) rule: apiGroups: ["apps"], resources: ["deployments"], verbs: ["list"]

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to allow reading Pods in the core API group:
  - apiGroups: [""]
  - resources: ["pods"]
  - verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already points to this Role and the pod-reader ServiceAccount, so no changes were needed there.

How to verify
- Can I check?  
  kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- List pods using that identity:  
  kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

You should now be able to list pods with the pod-reader service account in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: Service had no endpoints (Endpoints: <none>)
- The container listens on port 8080 (nginx-unprivileged image), but the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic to targetPort 80 would fail.

What I changed
- Updated the Service to select the correct Pods and route to the right port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: targetPort: 8080 (port stays 80 for clients)
- Verified Endpoints now show the Pod and port: 10.244.0.26:8080
- Verified in-cluster connectivity with a debug pod:
  - curl http://nginx and curl http://10.101.60.228 both return HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Current Service (fixed)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx
  namespace: web
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nginx
  ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8080

How you can double-check
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- kubectl -n web run tmp --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- \
  sh -lc 'curl -sS -I http://nginx && curl -sS -I http://$(kubectl -n web get svc nginx -o jsonpath={.spec.clusterIP})'

Notes
- If you need external access (outside the cluster), let me know and I can set up a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service or an Ingress.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: Service had no endpoints (Endpoints: <none>)
- The container listens on port 8080 (nginx-unprivileged image), but the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic to targetPort 80 would fail.

What I changed
- Updated the Service to select the correct Pods and route to the right port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: targetPort: 8080 (port stays 80 for clients)
- Verified Endpoints now show the Pod and port: 10.244.0.26:8080
- Verified in-cluster connectivity with a debug pod:
  - curl http://nginx and curl http://10.101.60.228 both return HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Current Service (fixed)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx
  namespace: web
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nginx
  ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8080

How you can double-check
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- kubectl -n web run tmp --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- \
  sh -lc 'curl -sS -I http://nginx && curl -sS -I http://$(kubectl -n web get svc nginx -o jsonpath={.spec.clusterIP})'

Notes

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: Service had no endpoints (Endpoints: <none>)
- The container listens on port 8080 (nginx-unprivileged image), but the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic to targetPort 80 would fail.

What I changed
- Updated the Service to select the correct Pods and route to the right port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: targetPort: 8080 (port stays 80 for clients)
- Verified Endpoints now show the Pod and port: 10.244.0.26:8080
- Verified in-cluster connectivity with a debug pod:
  - curl http://nginx and curl http://10.101.60.228 both return HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Current Service (fixed)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx
  namespace: web
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nginx
  ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8080

How you can double-check
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- kubectl -n web run tmp --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- \
  sh -lc 'curl -sS -I http://nginx && curl -sS -I http://$(kubectl -n web get svc nginx -o jsonpath={.spec.clusterIP})'

Notes
- If you need external access (outside the cluster), let me know and I can set up a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service or an Ingress.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis:
- Pods weren’t running because the Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but the cluster’s only node doesn’t have that label. The scheduler events show “0/1 nodes are available: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- Because no Pods could schedule, the Service web-app-service had no Endpoints, so clients saw “connection refused” when resolving web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local.

What I changed:
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
- Result:
  - Pods are now Running:
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-ztblh (10.244.0.32)
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-vh59s (10.244.0.33)
  - Service Endpoints are populated: 10.244.0.32:80, 10.244.0.33:80
  - EndpointSlice shows port 80 with the two endpoints.

Why this fixes the issue:
- With Pods running and Endpoints published, connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should now succeed instead of being refused.

Optional verification you can run:
- From your workstation (if kubectl access available):
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -o wide
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- From inside the cluster (temporary pod to test HTTP):
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl:8.8.0 --restart=Never -- sh -c 'curl -sSI http://web-app-service'
  - You should see HTTP/1.1 200 OK headers.

If you actually need to constrain to specific nodes:
- Add the proper label to the node: kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Or adjust the Deployment’s nodeSelector/affinity to match labels that exist.
- Consider adding readinessProbes so the Service only routes traffic when the container is ready.

Let me know if you want me to restore a specific scheduling constraint with a label you prefer, or to add probes.

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Diagnosis:
- Pods weren’t running because the Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but the cluster’s only node doesn’t have that label. The scheduler events show “0/1 nodes are available: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- Because no Pods could schedule, the Service web-app-service had no Endpoints, so clients saw “connection refused” when resolving web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local.

What I changed:
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
- Result:
  - Pods are now Running:
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-ztblh (10.244.0.32)
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-vh59s (10.244.0.33)
  - Service Endpoints are populated: 10.244.0.32:80, 10.244.0.33:80
  - EndpointSlice shows port 80 with the two endpoints.

Why this fixes the issue:
- With Pods running and Endpoints published, connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should now succeed instead of being refused.

Optional verification you can run:
- From your workstation (if kubectl access available):
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -o wide
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- From inside the cluster (temporary pod to test HTTP):
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl:8.8.0 --restart=Never -- sh -c 'curl -sSI http://web-app-service'
  - You should see HTTP/1.1 200 OK headers.

If you actually need to constrain to specific nodes:
- Add the proper label to the node: kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Or adjust the Deployment’s nodeSelector/affinity to match labels that exist.
- Consider adding readinessProbes so the Service only routes traffic when the container is ready.

Let me know if you want me to restore a specific scheduling constraint with a label you prefer, or to add probes.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis:
- Pods weren’t running because the Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but the cluster’s only node doesn’t have that label. The scheduler events show “0/1 nodes are available: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- Because no Pods could schedule, the Service web-app-service had no Endpoints, so clients saw “connection refused” when resolving web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local.

What I changed:
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
- Result:
  - Pods are now Running:
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-ztblh (10.244.0.32)
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-vh59s (10.244.0.33)
  - Service Endpoints are populated: 10.244.0.32:80, 10.244.0.33:80
  - EndpointSlice shows port 80 with the two endpoints.

Why this fixes the issue:
- With Pods running and Endpoints published, connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should now succeed instead of being refused.

Optional verification you can run:
- From your workstation (if kubectl access available):
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -o wide
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- From inside the cluster (temporary pod to test HTTP):
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl:8.8.0 --restart=Never -- sh -c 'curl -sSI http://web-app-service'
  - You should see HTTP/1.1 200 OK headers.

If you actually need to constrain to specific nodes:
- Add the proper label to the node: kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Or adjust the Deployment’s nodeSelector/affinity to match labels that exist.
- Consider adding readinessProbes so the Service only routes traffic when the container is ready.

Let me know if you want me to restore a specific scheduling constraint with a label you prefer, or to add probes.

- Increased PVC storage request from 1Gi to 3Gi for PVC storage-pvc used by Pod storage-pod in namespace resize-pv.
- Restarted the pod to complete the filesystem resize (the CSI driver reported FileSystemResizePending).

Current state
- PVC resize-pv/storage-pvc
  - requested: 3Gi
  - capacity: 3Gi
  - status: Bound
- PV pvc-f587b91a-5d8a-4f2d-9e0d-820c51ae7583
  - capacity: 3Gi
- Pod resize-pv/storage-pod
  - Running
  - PVC mounted at /usr/share/nginx/html

How to verify
- kubectl -n resize-pv get pvc storage-pvc -o jsonpath='{.status.capacity.storage}'; echo
- kubectl -n resize-pv exec -it storage-pod -- df -h /usr/share/nginx/html

Note: The pod was briefly restarted to complete the node filesystem resize as required by the hostpath CSI driver. Data on the PVC was preserved.

namespace/resize-pv created
persistentvolumeclaim/storage-pvc created
pod/storage-pod created

Done.

What I changed

- Restarted the pod to complete the filesystem resize (the CSI driver reported FileSystemResizePending).

Current state
- PVC resize-pv/storage-pvc
  - requested: 3Gi
  - capacity: 3Gi
  - status: Bound
- PV pvc-f587b91a-5d8a-4f2d-9e0d-820c51ae7583
  - capacity: 3Gi
- Pod resize-pv/storage-pod
  - Running
  - PVC mounted at /usr/share/nginx/html

How to verify
- kubectl -n resize-pv get pvc storage-pvc -o jsonpath='{.status.capacity.storage}'; echo
- kubectl -n resize-pv exec -it storage-pod -- df -h /usr/share/nginx/html

Note: The pod was briefly restarted to complete the node filesystem resize as required by the hostpath CSI driver. Data on the PVC was preserved.
